subtype: Returning to India after years abroad [Actor]
passage: Thomas, listen. I came back to Bengaluru at twenty after five years in Perth, and I expected to slide right in. Instead the city had moved without me: the lane had a new flyover, my friends had new jokes and I didn't know the auto fare. Worse, I had changed too. The noise was too much and my Kannada slow. I felt like a guest in my own house. My mother said, "Give it time. You're not late." I began small: I took the bus with a route written on my hand, went to the same bakery every Saturday, and asked my old friend to explain the jokes instead of pretending. After some months I noticed I'd stopped feeling out of step. Nobody handed me a place. I built one slowly. Anjali

qa.q: How many years had Anjali spent in Perth?
qa.a: Anjali spent five years in Perth.

qa.q: How did Anjali feel back in Bengaluru?
qa.a: Anjali felt lost and out of step, like a guest in the family home, since both the city and Anjali had changed.

qa.q: What choices helped Anjali, and why?
qa.a: Asking an old friend to explain the jokes instead of pretending, and building small routines like the bakery, so belonging grew slowly.

qa.q: What did Anjali's mother mean by You're not late?
qa.a: That there was no deadline for fitting in, and patience with the place and oneself was enough.

grounding: A young adult back in India after years abroad finds home changed and feels out of step, and patience brings a new fit.

subtype: Returning to India after years abroad [Actor]
passage: Nikita landed in Pune after six years in Toronto, and her suitcase did not. The airline said tomorrow. Outside, monsoon rain hammered the taxi rank, drivers shouted prices in Marathi that Nikita understood but answered slowly, and the phone was almost dead. Cousin Kalyani finally found Nikita under the shed. "You look lost," Kalyani said, laughing gently. Nikita's eyes stung. The city had rebuilt itself, and the road to the old school now had a metro pillar in the middle. Even Nikita's own jokes sounded odd in this air. "I don't know who I am here," Nikita said in the car. Kalyani answered, "You're the one who ate all the mango pickle, remember? Give it a week. You'll get the auto rates back." Nikita smiled at the windshield.

qa.q: What did the airline say about the suitcase?
qa.a: The airline said tomorrow.

qa.q: What was Nikita feeling in the car, and what shows it?
qa.a: Lost and out of step; Nikita's eyes stung and Nikita said not knowing who Nikita is here.

qa.q: What small step could help Nikita fit in again?
qa.a: Give it a week, relearn the auto rates and let familiar things like the mango pickle return.

qa.q: How might Kalyani see Nikita?
qa.a: As a familiar cousin beneath the changes who needs time; Kalyani laughed gently and recalled the mango pickle.

grounding: A young adult back in India after years abroad finds home changed and feels out of step, and patience begins a new fit.

subtype: Returning to India after years abroad [Actor]
passage:
The girls' hostel at the Pune college was noisy, hot and full of rules Tanuja didn't know. She had spent eight years in Singapore and came back at nineteen to study architecture. The first week, she queued for the bathroom and someone cut in; she said "excuse me, there's a queue" and got a stare. The canteen food made her stomach ache. She didn't get half the jokes. The city she remembered from childhood holidays had metro lines and malls now. Worse, she had changed too. She missed the order and felt guilty for missing it.
Her roommate Rajni, from Nashik, found her crying over instant noodles on the balcony. "Give it a month," Rajni said. "Also, come with me to the vada pav stall. It fixes everything." Tanuja went. The next week she bargained for a lamp in the market and won. Slowly, the noise started sounding like home.

qa.q: Where had Tanuja spent eight years?
qa.a: In Singapore.

qa.q: How was Tanuja feeling in her first week at the hostel?
qa.a: She felt out of step and homesick, and guilty for missing Singapore's order, even crying on the balcony.

qa.q: What did Rajni offer that helped Tanuja?
qa.a: Patience and company: she said to give it a month and took her to the vada pav stall, helping her take small steps into the new life.

qa.q: How might Rajni have seen Tanuja on the balcony?
qa.a: Rajni probably felt sympathetic and kind, seeing a homesick roommate who needed a friend more than advice.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult back in India who finds the place and herself changed and slowly finds a new fit with patience.

subtype: Returning to India after years abroad [Actor]
passage:
Dear Francis,
Six weeks back in Kolkata and I owe you a proper letter. You asked if it feels like home. Honestly? Not yet. The para I grew up in has three new flyovers and my favourite phuchka man has gone. My cousins talk about serials I've never seen. When I say "cheers" instead of "thank you", my aunts giggle. And I've changed too: I miss quiet, I miss queues, I miss being able to walk at night without a hundred questions.
I spent the first month annoyed at everything, mostly myself. Then Dida said something at dinner: "You went away a boy, you came back a man. The city also grew. Give each other time." So I'm trying. I've started morning walks by the lake with Dida. I've found a new phuchka man, nearly as good. I laugh at the serials with my cousins now, sometimes.
Write soon. Tell Toronto I miss it.
Nilesh

qa.q: What has happened to Nilesh's favourite phuchka man?
qa.a: He has gone.

qa.q: How did Nilesh feel during the first month back in Kolkata?
qa.a: Nilesh felt out of step and annoyed at everything, mostly at himself.

qa.q: What did Dida's advice encourage Nilesh to do?
qa.a: To be patient with both himself and the city, since both had changed, which led to morning walks and small new routines.

qa.q: How might Francis feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Francis might feel both missed and glad that Nilesh is slowly finding a new fit back home.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult back in India who finds home and himself changed, and finds a new fit through patience.

subtype: Returning to India after years abroad [Actor]
passage: Zainab, thanks for asking me on the podcast. I'm Abhinav, twenty-two, and I came back to Lucknow last year after eight years in Ohio. I thought I was coming home. But home had moved on. My school friends had jobs, some were married. The street where we played cricket is now a parking lot. And I had changed. I got upset when people didn't wait their turn. I said "sorry" too much. My uncles asked why I was so quiet, and my accent made shopkeepers double the price. For months I felt like a guest in my own city, and honestly I was grumpy with everyone. What helped was a small thing. My nani asked me to take her to the old market every Sunday. Slowly, I learnt the new lanes, and the shopkeepers learnt my face. It's taken a year. I fit differently now, but I fit.

qa.q: Where did Abhinav live for eight years?
qa.a: In Ohio.

qa.q: How did Abhinav feel in the first months back in Lucknow?
qa.a: Abhinav felt like a guest in the city, out of step and grumpy with everyone.

qa.q: What small routine helped Abhinav, and why?
qa.a: Taking nani to the old market every Sunday; the regular visits let Abhinav learn the new lanes and let shopkeepers get to know Abhinav over time.

qa.q: How might Abhinav's nani see those Sunday trips?
qa.a: She probably enjoyed the company and may have wanted to help Abhinav settle back in, gently easing the grandchild into the city.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult back in India who finds home and self changed, and slowly finds a new fit through patience.

subtype: Returning to India after years abroad [Actor]
passage:
Week one. Noor stood in the Aminabad lane where the old bookshop used to be; it was a phone-cover shop now. Pranav, her childhood neighbour, no longer waited for her in the park; he had a job and a moustache. She went home and cried into a pillow that no longer felt like hers, missing Dubai and missing a Lucknow that had quietly disappeared while she was gone.
Week four. The auto driver laughed at the way she bargained. She laughed too, eventually. She began walking in the early mornings, when the streets were slow enough to relearn.
Week nine. Pranav's mother sent kebabs over, and Pranav came along with them. "You've changed," he said. "So has the city," she answered. They sat on the roof arguing about which had changed more, and for the first time since landing, the evening felt like hers.

qa.q: What had the old bookshop in the Aminabad lane become?
qa.a: It was a phone-cover shop now.

qa.q: Why did Noor cry in the first week?
qa.a: She felt lonely and out of step, missing Dubai and also missing a Lucknow that had changed while she was away.

qa.q: What small habit helped Noor fit back in?
qa.a: Walking in the early mornings, when the streets were slow enough to relearn, gave her patient, gentle practice with the changed city.

qa.q: How might Pranav see Noor's return?
qa.a: Pranav notices she has changed, yet he still comes over with the kebabs and sits arguing on the roof, so he seems glad to reconnect.

grounding: Shows a young adult back in India after years abroad feeling out of step with a changed city and a changed self, and finding a new fit through patience.
